blocks.text: About Part 3b

This guide covers salaried and full-time employees. It is the second of the three reconciliation guides: Part 3a covers casuals, and Part 3c covers employees who need manual handling. It ends with a worked example of a correction you will meet often.

blocks.label: Different rules entirely.
blocks.text: Full-time and salaried staff are not treated under the Live Performance Award. CTS pays above award and applies its own overtime matrix instead. Applying casual award rules to a salaried employee will produce the wrong pay.
A full-time employee's fortnight should come to exactly 80 hours, unless there is approved overtime that has been pre-approved by their manager.
That figure is the anchor for everything else in this guide. If the total is not 80, something needs finding, and it is usually the rounding rule below rather than a genuine shortfall.

There is a preset rule in the Employment Hero back end that caps each salaried employee's captured hours at eight per day. It was created when CTS migrated from ADP to Employment Hero and applies to salaried employees only.

blocks.label: It rounds in both directions.
blocks.text: The rule does not simply cap long days. It also rounds short days up. If someone works less than eight hours on a day, Employment Hero will still record eight. This is the single biggest source of confusion when a total does not reconcile.

The practical consequence is that the pay run total and the real timesheet total can differ even when nothing is wrong. So you cannot reconcile from the pay run alone; you have to open the timesheets and compare day by day.
Work through the days that ran longer than eight hours and check what the pay run actually captured for each. Where it captured eight and the timesheet shows more, add the difference back.

blocks.caption: Permanent Ordinary Hours rows for a salaried employee, including a Time in lieu taken row. Rates and amounts are blurred in this guide.

blocks.label: Managers sometimes balance days themselves.
blocks.text: A manager may deliberately put four hours over on one day and four hours under on another so the fortnight still comes to 80. Before chasing a shortfall, check the week-ending view to see whether it has already been balanced out elsewhere in the fortnight.
Where overtime is genuinely payable, the rate comes from the internal CTS Overtime Matrix rather than the award. The matrix is held in the HR Resource Library on SharePoint.

blocks.caption: The CTS Overtime Matrix for full-time staff, with its legend.

blocks.text: Reading the matrix takes two pieces of information: which row the shift falls into, and which column applies to the fortnight:

rows: The nature of the shift: normal weekday, weekend (WE), before 5am or after 10pm (5 10), more than 12 hours in a day (>12), public holiday (PH), or a combination
Whether the fortnight is at or under 80 hours or above it, and whether the client is paying a higher rate than normal for the work
Mean the work is chargeable to the client at a higher rate, not simply that money is involved

blocks.text: So a shift worked between 10pm and 10:45pm, in a fortnight within 80 hours, chargeable to the client, falls in the 5 10 row against the chargeable column, giving 1.25.
To apply it, use Actions › Add earnings and pick the matching category, such as permanent overtime at 1.25. Copy across the notes so the reason is recorded against the entry.
Time in lieu taken is a form of leave, and must be populated in the In Lieu Taken column of the spreadsheet rather than left in ordinary hours.

blocks.label: The rest calculates itself.
blocks.text: Once you populate the leave columns, the remaining ordinary hours follow automatically: the formula takes 80 hours and subtracts whatever you have entered across columns F to S. Do not type the ordinary hours in by hand.

Where an employee accrues and takes time in lieu within the same fortnight and the two cancel out, the totals will still reconcile. Even so, record it properly and add a note explaining the offset, so that someone reading the fortnight later can see what happened.

Salaried employees often carry standing arrangements set up in their employee profile under pay run inclusions, most commonly a pre-tax salary sacrifice for technology, or a superannuation salary sacrifice.

blocks.caption: The pay run employee list, from which each employee's detail is opened. Names and pay figures are blurred in this guide.

blocks.text: These deduct automatically each fortnight and stop on their own, so they need checking rather than adjusting. There are two ways they can be set to end:

rows: The deduction stops once the nominated total has been reached. Preferred for technology salary sacrifice.
The deduction stops on a set date. Preferred for superannuation salary sacrifice.

blocks.label: Check it is still within its nominated period.
blocks.text: An arrangement that has passed its end date but is still active will keep deducting. Confirm against what the employee set out on their nominated form.

blocks.title: Apply any back pay from the payroll notes

blocks.text: Where the payroll notes from Part 1 record a back pay for this employee, add it now using Actions › Add earnings with the category the overtime matrix gives you, and copy the note across so the reason travels with the entry.
Record the same back pay in the spreadsheet against the employee, in the back pay column on the right.
Worked example: an overtime category triggered in error
The rest of this guide is a worked example taken from a real fortnight. It covers a salaried employee whose overtime category was applied automatically when it should not have been.

It is worth reading even if nothing like it is on your current pay run, because the trap at the centre of it, losing the notes when you change a category, applies to every correction you make in a pay run.
Recognise an incorrectly triggered overtime category

Employment Hero applies award conditions automatically. One of these flags any shift starting less than ten hours after the previous one ended, and reclassifies those hours into a higher-paid break category.

In the example, an employee finished at 8:00pm on 10 August and started again at 5:30am on 11 August. That gap is under ten hours, so Employment Hero moved the affected hours into the category shown below.

blocks.caption: Rows reclassified as 'Permanent - Less than 10 hrs break' sitting alongside normal 'Permanent Ordinary Hours'. Rates and amounts are blurred in this guide.

blocks.label: Salaried employees are not eligible.
blocks.text: Because CTS pays above award, a salaried employee does not attract this overtime. The category applies a substantially higher hourly rate, so leaving it in place overpays them. These rows must be changed back to Permanent Ordinary Hours.
Check the employment type before acting. This correction applies to salaried employees; it is not a blanket rule for everyone the break condition flags.
Copy the notes before you change anything
This is the step that catches people out, and there is no undo for it.

blocks.label: Changing the category wipes the notes.
blocks.text: The moment you change the category on a row, Employment Hero overwrites whatever was in that row's Notes field. Copy the note text out first, change the category, then paste it back. If you change the category first, the note is gone and you will have to reconstruct it from the timesheet.

blocks.caption: Selecting the Notes text to copy before touching the category dropdown. Names, rates and amounts are blurred in this guide.

blocks.text: For each affected row, work in this order:
Select and copy the contents of the Notes field
Change the category dropdown to Permanent Ordinary Hours
Paste the note back into the Notes field
Confirm the hours on the row are still correct
Repeat for every row carrying the break category. In the example there were four.
Re-check the total hours against the timesheets

Once the categories are corrected the employee's total will often sit below the expected 80 hours for a full-time fortnight. The reclassification changes how hours were captured, so they need checking against the source.
Open the employee's timesheets for the period and work through the days that are actually longer than eight hours; those are where the discrepancies sit.

blocks.caption: Timesheet Approval showing each day's real duration, including breaks. The employee name is blurred in this guide.

blocks.text: Compare each of those days against what the pay run captured, and correct the hours where they differ. In the example the pay run had captured eight hours for 12 August where the timesheet showed ten, and two later days were each short by an hour or more.

blocks.label: Work to the expected total.
blocks.text: Keep correcting until the total reaches the hours the employee is contracted for across the fortnight, 80 for a full-time employee. If you cannot reconcile to that figure, stop and investigate rather than adjusting a number to make it balance.
Confirm the corrected total and check leave
With the categories fixed and the hours corrected, the employee's line should show the expected total and every row should sit on the ordinary hours rate.

blocks.caption: The same employee after correction: 80 hours, all rows on Permanent Ordinary Hours. Names, rates and amounts are blurred in this guide.

blocks.text: Then check whether any leave was taken during the period, and populate the spreadsheet if so.

blocks.label: Leave taken, not leave accrued.
blocks.text: These are different things and only one matters here. Leave accrued is what the employee earned over the period and needs no action. Leave taken is what they actually used, and that does need populating. In the example there was leave accrued but none taken, so no entry was required.
Check pay run inclusions
Finally, check the employee's pay run inclusion settings for any standing arrangements, most commonly a superannuation salary sacrifice.

These carry nominated start and end dates, and they must match what the employee set out on their nominated form. In the example the sacrifice ran from 15 June through to the end of the financial year.

blocks.label: Check the dates, not just the amount.
blocks.text: A salary sacrifice that has passed its nominated end date but is still active will keep deducting. Confirm the arrangement is still within its nominated period for the fortnight you are processing.
Checklist
For each salaried or full-time employee:
The fortnight reconciles to 80 hours, or the excess is approved overtime
Days over eight hours checked against the timesheet, not just the pay run
Short days checked for the rounding rule rounding them up to eight
The week-ending view checked before chasing an apparent shortfall
Any overtime rated from the CTS Overtime Matrix, not the award
Time in lieu taken recorded in the leave column, with ordinary hours left to the formula
Pay run inclusions still within their nominated amount or date
Any back pay from the payroll notes added and recorded in the spreadsheet
Notes were copied before any category was changed, and pasted back afterwards
Any incorrectly triggered overtime category has been returned to Permanent Ordinary Hours
Any leave taken during the period has been populated in the spreadsheet
